event_date_basis: Three distinct dates, all first-party. (1) ISSUANCE / SIGNATURE = 2026-03-17: the document's own signature block reads 'By the Commissions. / Dated: March 17, 2026.' over Vanessa A. Countryman, Secretary, SEC and Christopher Kirkpatrick, Secretary, CFTC; the two CFR interpretative-release tables it adds also carry 'March 17, 2026' for Release Nos. 33-11412 and 34-105020; and the CFTC's own press release 9198-26 is dated March 17, 2026 and says the CFTC 'joined the Securities and Exchange Commission today in issuing an interpretation'. So the 3/17 date the law-firm summaries used is NOT media-only - it is in the official text. (2) FILING with the Office of the Federal Register = 2026-03-20: the closing line reads '[FR Doc. 2026-05635 Filed 3-20-26; 8:45 am]' (the PDF's internal creation timestamp is D:20260320231147Z, consistent). (3) PUBLICATION AND EFFECT = 2026-03-23: Federal Register Vol. 91, No. 55 (Monday, March 23, 2026), 91 FR 13714, and 'DATES: Effective Date: March 23, 2026.' The effective date is therefore NOT separate from the publication date - they are the same day. Note for the writing agent: the federalregister.gov API 'signing_date' field is null for this document; the 3/17 date must be taken from the document text and the CFTC press release, not from that field. The assigned slug fixes the event date at 2026-03-23 (publication + effect); this is defensible, but BRIEF.md says the slug date is the event day and batch 3 renamed a slug for exactly this reason, so if the orchestrator prefers the day the agencies acted, the slug would be ...-20260317. Flagged, not decided here. Whichever is chosen, news_date must equal the slug tail, and the article must state both dates explicitly.

verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Application of the Federal Securities Laws to Certain Types of Crypto Assets and Certain Transactions Involving Crypto Assets. | 33-11412 | March 17, 2026 | [INSERT Federal Register DOCUMENT CITATION]

verified_facts.fact: The CFTC announced the interpretation on March 17, 2026 in press release 9198-26, titled 'CFTC Joins SEC to Clarify the Application of Federal Securities Laws to Crypto Assets', which states the agencies issued it that day.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission joined the Securities and Exchange Commission today in issuing an interpretation clarifying how the federal securities laws apply to certain crypto assets and transactions involving crypto assets.

verified_facts.fact: On 2026-03-17 the CFTC said the document had not yet appeared in the Federal Register.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: The interpretation will be published on CFTC.gov and in the Federal Register.

verified_facts.fact: The two agencies play different roles inside the one document: the SEC issues the interpretation, and the CFTC provides guidance alongside it. The SUMMARY also states that 'we' and 'our' in the release mean the SEC only.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: SUMMARY: The Securities and Exchange Commission ("Commission" or "SEC") issues herein an interpretation regarding the application of the Federal securities laws to certain types of crypto assets and certain transactions involving crypto assets. The references in this release to "we" and "our" are to the Commission. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission ("CFTC") provides herein guidance relating to that interpretation.

verified_facts.fact: The CFTC's guidance is that it and its staff will administer the Commodity Exchange Act consistent with the SEC's interpretation, and that certain non-security crypto assets could meet the Commodity Exchange Act definition of 'commodity'.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Further, the CFTC provides herein guidance that the CFTC and its staff will administer the Commodity Exchange Act consistent with the interpretation, and that certain non-security crypto assets could meet the definition of "commodity" under the Commodity Exchange Act.

verified_facts.fact: A footnote states the release changes neither agency's statutory authority.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Nothing in this release should be construed as altering the respective statutory authorities of the SEC or CFTC.

verified_facts.fact: A further footnote limits the commodity point: any non-security crypto asset OTHER THAN a payment stablecoin issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer could meet the Commodity Exchange Act definition of 'commodity' (7 U.S.C. 1a(9)).
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: However, any non-security crypto asset, other than a "payment stablecoin issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer," as such terms are defined in section 2 of the GENIUS Act, could meet the definition of "commodity" under the Commodity Exchange Act. See 7 U.S.C. 1a(9).

verified_facts.fact: The release sorts crypto assets into five categories.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: For purposes of this release, we classify crypto assets into five categories based on their characteristics, uses, and functions: (i) digital commodities; (ii) digital collectibles; (iii) digital tools; (iv) stablecoins; and (v) digital securities.

verified_facts.fact: The legal status attached to each category: digital commodities, digital collectibles and digital tools are not themselves securities; stablecoins may or may not be, depending on their characteristics; digital securities are securities. A non-security crypto asset can still be offered and sold subject to an investment contract, which is a security.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Digital commodities, digital collectibles, and digital tools, each as further described below, are not themselves securities. However, as with any asset that is not a security, a non-security crypto asset can be offered and sold subject to an investment contract, which is a security. Stablecoins, as further described below, are a broad category of crypto assets that may or may not be securities depending on their characteristics. Digital securities, as further described below, are securities.

verified_facts.fact: The release warns its own taxonomy is not exhaustive: there may be crypto assets that fall in none of the five categories, and hybrid assets that fall in more than one.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Given the variations in crypto assets and the constantly evolving nature of the crypto asset markets, including the underlying technology, there may be crypto assets that do not fall within any of these five categories, as well as crypto assets with hybrid characteristics that may fall within more than one category.

verified_facts.fact: Definition of a digital commodity: a crypto asset intrinsically linked to and deriving its value from the programmatic operation of a 'functional' crypto system and from supply and demand, rather than from the expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others, and which has no intrinsic economic properties or rights such as generating a passive yield or conveying rights to future income, profits or assets of a business enterprise.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: A digital commodity is a crypto asset that is intrinsically linked to and derives its value from the programmatic operation of a crypto system that is "functional," as well as supply and demand dynamics, rather than from the expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

verified_facts.fact: The release names 16 assets as examples of digital commodities.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Examples of digital commodities include Aptos (APT); Avalanche (AVAX); Bitcoin (BTC); Bitcoin Cash (BCH); Cardano (ADA); Chainlink (LINK); Dogecoin (DOGE); Ether (ETH); Hedera (HBAR); Litecoin (LTC); Polkadot (DOT); Shiba Inu (SHIB); Solana (SOL); Stellar (XLM); Tezos (XTZ); and XRP (XRP).

verified_facts.fact: The naming is time-bound and explained: the conclusion rests on the Commission's understanding of each asset's characteristics, terms and functions 'as of the date of this release'; those 16 were chosen because each underlies a futures contract made available to trade on a CFTC-regulated designated contract market, which the release says is NOT a requirement; Algorand (ALGO) and LBRY Credits (LBC) are given as digital commodities that do not underlie such a futures contract.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Based on our understanding of their characteristics, terms, and functions as of the date of this release, the Commission concludes that each of these crypto assets is a digital commodity ... To be clear, it is not necessary that a crypto asset underlie such a futures contract to be a digital commodity; rather, the fact that these digital commodities underlie such a futures contract explains their selection as examples for this release.

verified_facts.fact: Definition of a digital collectible: a crypto asset designed to be collected and/or used, which may represent or convey rights to artwork, music, videos, trading cards, in-game items, or digital representations of internet memes, characters, current events or trends. Named examples: CryptoPunks, Chromie Squiggles, Fan Tokens, WIF and VCOIN. A meme coin is treated as a type of digital collectible with limited or no functionality.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: A digital collectible is a crypto asset that is designed to be collected and/or used and may represent or convey rights to artwork, music, videos, trading cards, in-game items, or digital representations or references to internet memes, characters, current events, or trends, among other things.

verified_facts.fact: Two qualifications on digital collectibles: an automated creator royalty paid on each resale does not turn a digital collectible into a security, but the offer and sale of a FRACTIONALISED digital collectible could be the offer or sale of a security because it may involve essential managerial efforts from which a purchaser would reasonably expect profits.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: the offer and sale of a digital collectible that either is fractionalized or otherwise enables individuals to acquire a fractional ownership interest of a single digital collectible, could constitute the offer or sale of a security

verified_facts.fact: The release also says a crypto asset first sold as a meme coin with no functionality can LATER become a digital commodity if it becomes functional within an associated functional crypto system - the categories are not permanent.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: a crypto asset may be offered and sold initially as a meme coin ... but later become a digital commodity because it becomes functional within an associated functional crypto system

verified_facts.fact: Definition of a digital tool: a crypto asset that performs a practical function such as a membership, ticket, credential, title instrument or identity badge; often non-transferrable or 'soul-bound'. Named examples: Ethereum Name Service domain names and CoinDesk's 'Microcosms' NFT Consensus Ticket.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: A digital tool is a crypto asset that performs a practical function, such as a membership, ticket, credential, title instrument, or identity badge.

verified_facts.fact: Stablecoins: the GENIUS Act (Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act, Public Law 119-27, 139 Stat. 419 (2025)) was enacted in July 2025; its section 17 excludes a 'payment stablecoin issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer' from the definition of 'security'; section 2(22) defines 'payment stablecoin'; section 2(23) defines 'permitted payment stablecoin issuer' as a person formed in the United States that is a subsidiary of an insured depository institution approved under section 5, a Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer, or a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: The GENIUS Act excludes from the definition of "security" any "payment stablecoin issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer," as such terms are defined in section 2 of the GENIUS Act.

verified_facts.fact: Section 4(a)(11) of the GENIUS Act bars a permitted payment stablecoin issuer from paying any form of interest or yield to holders, in cash, tokens or other consideration, solely in connection with holding, using or retaining the payment stablecoin.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: A permitted payment stablecoin issuer is prohibited under the GENIUS Act from paying any form of interest or yield to the permitted stablecoin holders (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of the payment stablecoin.

verified_facts.fact: The GENIUS Act was still not in force when the interpretation issued: it becomes effective on the earlier of 18 months after its date of enactment (stated as July 18, 2025) or 120 days after the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators issue any final implementing regulations. No fixed calendar date is given.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: The GENIUS Act will become effective on the earlier of 18 months after its date of enactment (July 18, 2025) or the date that is 120 days after the date on which the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators issue any final regulations implementing the GENIUS Act.

verified_facts.fact: Because the GENIUS Act was not yet effective, the Commission interpreted that the offer and sale of 'Covered Stablecoins' as described in the Division of Corporation Finance's Staff Statement on Stablecoins (April 4, 2025) does not involve the offer and sale of securities under Securities Act section 2(a)(1) or Exchange Act section 3(a)(10), so issuance and redemption need not be registered; the interpretation expressly does not address stablecoins other than Covered Stablecoins.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: the Commission interprets that, for the reasons set forth in the Staff Stablecoin Statement, the offer and sale of Covered Stablecoins does not involve the offer and sale of securities ... The foregoing interpretation does not address stablecoins other than Covered Stablecoins as described in the Staff Stablecoin Statement.

verified_facts.fact: Definition of a digital security (commonly called a tokenized security): a financial instrument enumerated in the definition of 'security' that is formatted as or represented by a crypto asset, with ownership recorded in whole or in part on one or more crypto networks. The release states the format does not matter.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: A security is a security regardless of whether it is issued, or otherwise represented, offchain or onchain. All devices and instruments that have the economic characteristics of a security are securities regardless of format or label.

verified_facts.fact: Section IV sets out when a non-security crypto asset becomes subject to an investment contract: when an issuer offers it by inducing an investment of money in a common enterprise with representations or promises to undertake essential managerial efforts from which a purchaser would reasonably expect to derive profits.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: A non-security crypto asset becomes subject to an investment contract when an issuer offers it by inducing an investment of money in a common enterprise with representations or promises to undertake essential managerial efforts from which a purchaser would reasonably expect to derive profits.

verified_facts.fact: Whose words count: representations or promises made by or on behalf of the issuer and conveyed to purchasers can create reasonable profit expectations; those made by third parties such as unaffiliated proponents or holders cannot, unless authorised by the issuer and conveyed to purchasers. Timing also matters - the issuer's POST-sale representations do not convert a prior sale into the sale of an investment contract.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: As such, the issuer's post-sale representations or promises would not convert the prior sale into an offer or sale of an investment contract.

verified_facts.fact: Channels that count for such representations include written or oral agreements, public communications through which the issuer has established a regular pattern of communicating (its website or official social media accounts), direct private communications, regulatory filings publicly available to purchasers, and documents clearly attributable to the issuer such as a whitepaper.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: public communications through which the issuer has established a regular pattern of communicating (such as the issuer's website or official social media accounts)

verified_facts.fact: Detail matters: representations with detailed milestones, a timeline, personnel, funding and an explanation of how holders will profit likely create a reasonable expectation of profit; vague statements with no semblance of an actionable business plan likely do not.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: In contrast, representations or promises that are vague or contain no semblance of an actionable business plan, such as those lacking milestones, funding, or other plans for needed resources, likely would not create reasonable expectations of profit.

verified_facts.fact: Being subject to an investment contract does not make the crypto asset itself a security.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: the fact that a non-security crypto asset is subject to an investment contract does not transform the non-security crypto asset itself into a security

verified_facts.fact: Secondary market rule: a non-security crypto asset does not stay subject to the investment contract in secondary market transactions where purchasers would not reasonably expect the issuer's representations to remain connected to it; where they would, secondary market offers and sales are securities transactions that must be registered under the Securities Act or done under an available exemption.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Under such circumstances, secondary market offers and sales of such a non-security crypto asset would constitute securities transactions that must be registered under the Securities Act or conducted pursuant to an available exemption from registration.

verified_facts.fact: Two non-exclusive indicia of 'separation' from an investment contract: (1) FULFILMENT - the issuer has completed the essential managerial efforts it promised, even if it keeps doing non-essential work; (2) FAILURE - a purchaser would no longer reasonably expect the issuer to be able to fulfil or continue those efforts, for example after enough time has passed with nothing done, or where the issuer publicly announces it is abandoning development. The release says such an announcement must be widely disseminated and unambiguous.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: As discussed below, we would not expect a non-security crypto asset to be subject to an investment contract when any of the following non-exclusive indicia of separation is present.

verified_facts.fact: Separation does not erase past liability: if the offering of the investment contract was never registered or exempt, the issuer still violated the Securities Act and investors keep their rights, and the issuer may still be liable under the anti-fraud provisions for material misstatements or omissions, even after the investment contract ceases to exist.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: even if the non-security crypto asset subsequently separates from the associated investment contract and that investment contract ceases to exist

verified_facts.fact: Section V covers two activities: 'Protocol Mining' means mining digital commodities on public, permissionless proof-of-work networks, and 'Protocol Staking' means staking digital commodities on public, permissionless proof-of-stake networks.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: (1) certain digital commodity activities known as "mining" on public, permissionless crypto networks that use proof-of-work ("PoW") as a consensus mechanism ("PoW Networks"); and (2) certain digital commodity activities known as "staking" on public, permissionless crypto networks that use proof-of-stake ("PoS") as a consensus mechanism ("PoS Networks")

verified_facts.fact: Covered Protocol Mining is limited to two forms - Self (or Solo) Mining and Mining Pool, including the roles of mining pools and pool operators in earning and distributing rewards.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Only Protocol Mining Activities undertaken in connection with the following types of Protocol Mining are addressed in this release: Self (or Solo) Mining ... Mining Pool

verified_facts.fact: The interpretation on mining: Protocol Mining Activities, in the manner and circumstances described, do not involve the offer and sale of a security under Securities Act section 2(a)(1) or Exchange Act section 3(a)(10), so participants need not register those transactions or find an exemption. The reasoning is that mining is an administrative or ministerial activity and rewards are payments for services to the network, not profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Protocol Mining Activities, in the manner and under the circumstances described in this release, do not involve the offer and sale of a security within the meaning of section 2(a)(1) of the Securities Act and section 3(a)(10) of the Exchange Act.

verified_facts.fact: Covered Protocol Staking is limited to four arrangements: Self (or Solo) Staking; Self-Custodial Staking Directly with a Third Party; Custodial Arrangement; and Liquid Staking. Covered participants include third-party Node Operators, Validators, Custodians, Delegates, Nominators and Liquid Staking Providers, collectively 'Service Providers'.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: (2) the activities undertaken by third parties involved in the Protocol Staking process--including, but not limited to, third-party Node Operators, Validators, Custodians, Delegates, Nominators, and Liquid Staking Providers (collectively, "Service Providers")

verified_facts.fact: The interpretation on staking: Protocol Staking Activities, in the manner and circumstances described, do not involve the offer and sale of a security under Securities Act section 2(a)(1) or Exchange Act section 3(a)(10), so participants need not register those transactions or find an exemption.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Protocol Staking Activities, in the manner and under the circumstances described in this release, do not involve the offer and sale of a security within the meaning of section 2(a)(1) of the Securities Act or section 3(a)(10) of the Exchange Act.

verified_facts.fact: Four 'Ancillary Services' are named as administrative or ministerial and therefore inside the interpretation: Slashing Coverage (the provider reimburses or indemnifies against slashing loss); Early Unbonding (returning assets before the protocol's unbonding period ends); Alternate Rewards Payment Schedules and Amounts; and Aggregation of Digital Commodities to meet a protocol staking minimum.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Slashing Coverage ... Early Unbonding ... Alternate Rewards Payment Schedules and Amounts ... Aggregation of Digital Commodities

verified_facts.fact: The staking interpretation carries explicit boundary conditions. Alternate reward schedules are inside the release only 'provided the reward amounts are not fixed, guaranteed, or greater than those awarded by the PoS Network's software protocol'. Footnotes state that if a Custodian or a Liquid Staking Provider decides whether, when or how much of a depositor's digital commodities to stake, or guarantees or sets the amount of rewards owed, its activities are OUTSIDE the scope of the release. The release does not say such arrangements are securities - it says it does not address them.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: provided the reward amounts are not fixed, guaranteed, or greater than those awarded by the PoS Network's software protocol

verified_facts.fact: Staking Receipt Tokens: a receipt for a non-security crypto asset that is not subject to an investment contract is not a security, and that covers generating, issuing, redeeming and secondary market offers and sales; BUT a Staking Receipt Token that is a receipt for a digital security, or for a non-security crypto asset that IS subject to an investment contract, is a security.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: In contrast, the offer or sale of a Staking Receipt Token that is a receipt for a digital security or a non-security crypto asset that is subject to an investment contract is an offer or sale of a security within the meaning of section 2(a)(1) of the Securities Act or section 3(a)(10) of the Exchange Act.

verified_facts.fact: A footnote limits it further: where a Liquid Staking Provider provides the means by which a Staking Receipt Token can be used to generate additional returns, those activities are outside the scope of the release.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Where a Liquid Staking Provider provides the means by which such a Staking Receipt Token can be used to generate such returns, those activities are outside the scope of this release.

verified_facts.fact: Section VI covers 'wrapping': depositing a crypto asset with a Custodian or cross-chain bridge (the 'Wrapped Token Provider') which issues an equivalent amount of 'Redeemable Wrapped Tokens' one-for-one 'without directly or indirectly offering any return, yield, profit opportunity, or additional good or service'. The deposited asset is locked up and cannot be transferred, lent, pledged or rehypothecated, and the holder can redeem one-for-one, whereupon the wrapped tokens are burned. Same receipt logic as staking receipt tokens: a receipt for a non-security asset not subject to an investment contract is not a security; a receipt for a digital security or for an asset subject to an investment contract is.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: without directly or indirectly offering any return, yield, profit opportunity, or additional good or service

verified_facts.fact: Section VII covers airdrops, and only a narrow slice of them: airdrops of non-security crypto assets to recipients who give the issuer no money, goods, services or other consideration in exchange. In those circumstances the first element of the Howey test - an investment of money - is not met, so the asset does not become subject to an investment contract and the issuer need not register the transaction.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: this interpretation addresses only airdrops of non-security crypto assets by issuers to recipients who do not provide the issuer with money, goods, services, or other consideration in exchange for the airdropped non-security crypto assets

verified_facts.fact: The airdrop carve-outs are precise: the interpretation does NOT pertain where the recipient performs a service in exchange (the release gives following the issuer on social media, reposting, writing an article, referring someone, or fixing bugs as examples of such services); it DOES pertain where consideration was given before the airdrop was announced and no further consideration is required afterwards; if the issuer requires action after the announcement - buying a specified crypto asset, buying a good or service, or performing a task - the interpretation does not apply. It also does not address airdrops of digital securities.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: The interpretation does not pertain to any airdrops of non-security crypto assets where the recipient provides the issuer with money, goods, services, or other consideration in exchange for the airdropped non-security crypto asset, such as where the recipient performs a service in exchange for the airdropped non-security crypto asset.

verified_facts.fact: The airdrop interpretation is also limited going forward: a footnote notes an investment contract may exist in connection with other transactions involving the same asset before or after the airdrop, in which case a later transaction such as the recipient's secondary market sale could be a securities transaction requiring registration or an exemption.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: the non-security crypto asset disseminated in the airdrop may become subject to that investment contract in a subsequent transaction, which would constitute a securities transaction, such as where the airdrop recipient sells the non-security crypto asset in a secondary market transaction

verified_facts.fact: The interpretation is not a substitute for case law.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: The interpretation in this release does not supersede or replace the Howey test, which is binding legal precedent.

verified_facts.fact: The SEC states it and its staff will administer the Federal securities laws consistent with the interpretation, including in enforcement actions, and calls this a first step.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: The Commission and its staff will administer the Federal securities laws consistent with the interpretation, including with respect to enforcement actions. verified_facts.fact: Procedural status under the Congressional Review Act: OMB designated the interpretation a 'major rule' under 5 U.S.C. 804(2), yet it could take effect immediately under 5 U.S.C. 808(2) because it is an interpretive rule exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act's notice-and-comment requirements. It is also a significant regulatory action under section 3(f) of Executive Order 12866 and was reviewed by OMB. This is why the effective date equals the publication date.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Pursuant to the Congressional Review Act, the Office of Management and Budget ("OMB") has designated the interpretation in this release as a "major rule," as defined by 5 U.S.C. 804(2). Notwithstanding such designation, the interpretation in this release may take effect immediately pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 808(2) because it is an interpretive rule and thus exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act's notice and comment requirements.

editorial_brief: READER: Taiwanese readers who hold or use crypto through overseas platforms and keep seeing the headline '美國宣布多數加密資產不是證券', and who need to know what that sentence does and does not mean. They are not US lawyers and will not read a 20-page Federal Register release. ANGLE: three things the headline hides. (1) It is a JOINT SEC + CFTC document, not an SEC announcement - the SEC issues the interpretation and the CFTC issues guidance that it will administer the Commodity Exchange Act consistently with it, and the CFTC's own press release is the proof. (2) The date everyone quotes depends on which date they mean: signed 2026-03-17, filed 2026-03-20, published and effective 2026-03-23 - and the reason publication and effect fall on the same day is a procedural one worth one clear sentence (an interpretive rule, exempt from notice and comment, so it took effect immediately under 5 U.S.C. 808(2) despite OMB's 'major rule' designation). (3) '不是證券' is a jurisdiction-and-registration answer, not a safety answer: the same release keeps the anti-fraud provisions alive, keeps past registration failures actionable, says the categories can change, and expressly does not touch tax, anti-money-laundering rules, or any non-US law. STRUCTURE THAT FITS THE FIVE SECTIONS: what was issued and by whom; the three dates and what each one means (this is also where the table goes - a 3-4 column, 4-5 row table of date / what happened / what it is called in the document / where it appears); the five-category taxonomy and what 'not itself a security' actually decides (diagram section); the four activities the release covers - protocol mining, protocol staking, wrapping, airdrops - and the conditions attached to each; and what the release deliberately leaves alone. ORIGINAL SCENARIO (must be labelled as an editorially constructed example): a reader who uses an overseas platform's staking function reads that staking 'is not a securities transaction' and asks whether that means the platform is now supervised - the answer being that the release addresses a narrow set of arrangements, says nothing about whether any particular provider is registered or licensed, and expressly excludes arrangements where the provider guarantees or fixes rewards. DELIBERATELY NOT COVERED: prices and market reaction; which assets to hold; exchange comparisons; the GENIUS Act's implementation mechanics (that belongs to the C6-C9 articles); the August 2026 'Regulation Crypto Assets' proposal beyond one sentence pointing to it as a separate, later, still-only-proposed regime.

THE DIVIDING LINE: C3 is about what a crypto asset IS under the law as it already stands - an interpretation, joint, in force since 2026-03-23, creating no new obligations.
